Although two Army soldiers were killed, the evidence presented was circumstantial and insufficient. The court emphasized the necessity of legal proof despite the crime's severity and implications.

stories.headline: Delhi pollution: September deadline gone, Centre wants MRSMs on ‘war footing’
stories.title: Delhi pollution: September deadline gone, Centre wants MRSMs on ‘war footing’
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Since November 2025, the Centre has flagged the need to expand mechanised road sweeping and fix operational gaps in at least seven high-level meetings covering Delhi, records reviewed by The Indian Express show.

In May 2026, the Centre directed the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and the Delhi government to expedite procurement of “all remaining Mechanical Road Sweeping Machines (MRSMs)” and complete the process “by September”.
After the deadline was missed, the Centre said in a meeting held just four days ago that the MRSMs should be procured on a “war footing”.

At a review meeting on air pollution control in the region, chaired by Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav, CAQM was directed to ask municipal commissioners across the National Capital Region (NCR) to identify road categories according to their width and fix minimum MRSM deployment requirements for each.

CAQM was also asked to circulate best practices adopted by municipal corporations for tendering machines under an operating expenditure (OPEX) model, where recurring payments are made to the provider based on output, to speed up procurement.
An internal assessment at the time had identified 8,129 km of roads in Delhi for mechanised sweeping.
The meeting also called for a substantial increase in MRSM deployment to meet the requirement and cover smaller roads.

At a review meeting covering Delhi, UP, Haryana and Greater Noida, the MCD, NDMC (New Delhi Municipal Corporation) and the Public Works Department (PWD) were directed to assign an officer to each MRSM to monitor its efficiency and verify whether it was removing visible dust.
The monitoring mechanism was to include GPS tracking and recording the quantity of dust collected and handed over to the nearest construction and demolition waste collection and processing site.
The Delhi government and MCD were directed to prepare an action plan to increase the number of mechanical road sweepers from the existing 76 to 505.
The 505-machine requirement was based on the length and width of Delhi’s road network.

It comprised 246 small machines for 9,855 km of roads with a right of way (RoW) below 20 feet, 91 medium machines for 7,277 km of roads with a RoW of 20-60 feet, and 168 large machines for 13,409 km of roads with a RoW above 60 feet.

stories.headline: India, China hold 10-day talks to ease LAC tensions in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.title: India, China hold 10-day talks to ease LAC tensions in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.summary: The talks focused on establishing engagement protocols, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, and maintaining open communication channels
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India and China have concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks aimed at easing tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and putting in place measures to prevent friction between troops deployed along the frontier ahead of the onset of harsh winter conditions.
Sources in the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the closely guarded discussions, which began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between.
The talks were described as cordial, though it remains unclear whether the measures discussed will be implemented on the ground before winter sets in fully.
Lieutenant-General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps, also known as the Spear Corps, led the Indian delegation.
The formation is headquartered at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland.
His Chinese counterpart and other military officers participated in the discussions.
An official from the Ministry of External Affairs was also present.

The latest round of talks primarily focused on establishing engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, maintaining open communication channels and reducing tensions in the eastern sector.
Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.

The discussions assume significance as winter conditions along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh can become extremely severe, posing considerable challenges to troop sustenance, movement and logistical support.
Any delay in implementing the measures discussed could complicate the situation on the ground as temperatures fall and access to forward areas becomes increasingly difficult.
The second round follows the first Corps Commander-level meeting, held on September 6 and 7, 2026, at the Wacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting (BPM) point in the Kibithoo sector.

stories.headline: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.title: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.summary: Each previous instance coincided with extraordinary disruptions, from the Emergency and Lok Sabha dissolutions to Indira Gandhi’s assassination and the COVID-19 pandemic
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Winter Session of Parliament has been skipped only four times in India’s parliamentary history, and each instance was linked to exceptional circumstances, including the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

With the Monsoon Session yet to be prorogued, setting a record for Parliament remaining unprorogued for more than 100 days, speculation has grown over the possibility of a short special session to consider the delimitation Bill.
The absence of any move to summon Parliament for its customary winter sitting has also fuelled discussion about whether the session could be skipped altogether.
The first time Parliament missed its winter session was during the 19-month Emergency.
The Lok Sabha met from July 21 to August 7, 1975, and then only from January 5 to February 6, 1976, without sitting during November or December, when the Winter Session is normally held.
The next instance came in 1979 after the premature dissolution of the Sixth Lok Sabha on August 22.
The newly elected House met only in January 1980, resulting in the Winter Session being skipped.
A similar situation arose in 1984 following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31.
General elections were called, and the Eighth Lok Sabha held its first sitting on January 15, 1985.
After a gap of 36 years, the Winter Session was skipped again in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Amid fears over the spread of the virus and stringent social-distancing norms, Parliament did not meet after the truncated Monsoon Session that ran from September 14 to 23.
In the 12 years of the Narendra Modi government, the timing of the Winter Session has varied considerably.

stories.headline: Only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi? Supreme Court in favour of step to curb air pollution
stories.title: Only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi? Supreme Court in favour of step to curb air pollution
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday said it is in favour of allowing only vehicles compliant with BS-VI emission standards in Delhi and it would be an effective measure to combat air pollution in the city.

As a three-judge bench, presided by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, heard proceedings initiated suo motu by the top court to deal with the annual air pollution woes in the Capital, it underlined that Delhi had a “lucky winter” as the air pollution did not touch “Severe” levels this year.
BS-VI standards became mandatory across India on April 1, 2020, for manufacturing, sale, and registration of new vehicles.

During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, who was part of a three-judge bench said, “The BS-VI compliance must follow…and restricted not only to Delhi but to the entire National Capital Region (NCR).
That is one thing which will significantly contribute to reduction of (pollution).”
During the hearing, a counsel pointed out that the SC had — by an order dated December 17, 2025 — said that BS-IV vehicles would be permitted and that no coercive action should be taken against them.
“They have now stopped doing Pollution Under Control (PUC) certification of these vehicles.
Let them do the PUC,” the counsel urged the bench.
The CJI, however, said, “…Let the status quo remain for next month or so too.”
The counsel once again requested the court to allow PUC for BS-IV vehicles saying “because of that (not allowing PUC), these vehicles are not getting fuel.”
“That’s what we want.
We want that.

stories.headline: Political leaders, environmentalists seek ecological protection
stories.title: Political leaders, environmentalists seek ecological protection
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 23: Political leaders, environmentalists, and civil society groups on Monday called for an investigation into the use of heavy machinery near Sheshnag Lake, raising concerns over possible damage to the ecologically fragile glacial landscape. A video circulating on social media showing a crawler excavator digging and levelling ground near Sheshnag, a high-altitude glacial lake in south Kashmir's Pahalgam area, has triggered widespread concern and demands for an immediate halt to the activity. The footage shows the machine cutting into the ground, moving earth and dumping soil along the Amarnath Yatra route near the lake. Initially shared by an excavator operator before being deleted, the video has raised questions about the precise location and nature of the excavation, the agencies involved and its possible environmental impact. CPI(M) MLA from Kulgam Muhammad Yusuf Tarigami, who also chairs the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly's Committee on Environment, called for an immediate halt to the activity and an inspection by glaciologists and environmental experts. Expressing concern over videos purportedly showing heavy machinery being used for road development along the Amarnath Yatra track, Tarigami said Sheshnag was among the 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir. He said the lake was surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes, making the terrain particularly vulnerable to disturbance. "Disturbing this fragile terrain with heavy machinery is an invitation to disaster," Tarigami said in a statement. He said nobody was opposed to development and that pilgrims, tourists and local residents deserved better roads and facilities. However, infrastructure development in the high Himalayas must be guided by scientific studies, environmental impact assessments and consultations with experts and local communities. Referring to the 2013 Kedarnath disaster, the 2023 South Lhonak Lake disaster in Sikkim and a recent glacier-related disaster in Nepal, Tarigami cautioned against human interference in fragile mountain ecosystems. He warned that the potential consequences could extend downstream to Pahalgam, settlements along the Lidder and other parts of south Kashmir. Tarigami sought details of the project, the executing agency and the clearances obtained, besides an immediate halt to any work that could threaten the lake and its surroundings. "Development cannot and should not come at the cost of such a disaster," he said. Former chief minister and PDP President, Mehbooba Mufti, said the issue was very painful, and criticised the government for watching as mere spectators. "The government itself is having Chinar trees cut down. At the university, they are cutting down our old walnut trees. They just watch as spectators and don't say a word. Our Kashmir will become another Uttarakhand. What can we say? When they built roads and expressways for the Char Dham Yatra, look at how many storms and calamities strike there today. It is very bad," she said. "The issue is very painful." However, she said that if her party says anything more on the issue, it will be accused of being against the Amarnath Yatra. "If we talk about it, they will say we are against the Amarnath Yatra. What can I say? They try to polarise everything," she told reporters here. National Conference (NC) Lok Sabha MP Mian Altaf said it is essential to safeguard Kashmir's lakes. "I have not seen that, so I cannot say anything to you about it. I will just say that Kashmir's lakes must be saved. They must be saved at any cost. Its rivers must be saved, its forests must be saved. That is essential for all of us, essential for Kashmir, for Kashmir's tourism, for Kashmir's environment, and for our health," Altaf said. Apni Party President and former minister Altaf Bukhari said authorities must clarify whether the video showing a JCB operating near Sheshnag Lake was authentic. "If the video is genuine, the government owes the public a clear explanation: What is such heavy machinery doing in an ecologically fragile zone, especially around a high-altitude glacial lake?" he said. Bukhari said Kashmir had already suffered the consequences of unchecked construction and human interference, resulting in the loss of glaciers, water bodies and natural habitats. He said authorities must act responsibly, ensure transparency and protect the region's natural heritage, adding that development should not come at the cost of environmental destruction. Former Lok Sabha MP from Srinagar, Syed Aga Ruhullah, said Kashmir's mountains are not the BJP's real estate. "A party that wins votes in the name of faith is now taking JCBs to a holy lake. First, the BJP pushed motor roads up to the Amarnath cave. Now heavy machinery is digging at Sheshnag, a high-risk glacial lake. "Nepal just showed us what happens when the Himalaya is treated like a construction site. Stop this now. Kashmir's mountains are not BJP's real estate," Ruhullah said in a post on his official handle on X. Kashmir's chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq also termed the visuals disturbing, saying glacier retreat and recent glacier-related floods in neighbouring Nepal should serve as a warning about the vulnerability of the Himalayan region. "Kashmir has always warmly welcomed Amarnath Yatra pilgrims, and improving facilities for them has never been an issue. But not at the cost of our fragile ecosystem," Mirwaiz wrote on X. He demanded an immediate halt to the activity, saying the region's mountains, glaciers and water bodies needed protection for present and future generations. People's Democratic Party spokesperson Mohit Bhan described the reported activity as a "crime against Hinduism and faith in nature", citing Sheshnag's religious significance. According to Hindu belief, lord Shiva left behind the serpents at Sheshnag before proceeding towards the Amarnath Cave to narrate the Amar Katha to goddess Parvati. "There is a profound contradiction in invoking Hindu faith while allowing the very landscape associated with that faith to be disturbed through unnecessary construction, road cutting and surface levelling," Bhan said. "Faith and ecology are not competing interests. Both demand protection," he said, adding that development should not come at the cost of the fragile alpine ecosystem or the religious significance of the yatra route. Environmentalist Nikhil Saini sought clarity on the purpose of the work, saying construction could be justified if required for defence purposes or critical emergency connectivity, but otherwise raised serious concerns. "We've seen enough disasters over the years to understand how fragile mountain terrain is. At some point, we really need to question whether such constructions are even worth it," he said. Climate activist and RTI campaigner Raja Muzaffar Bhat questioned how heavy machinery had reached the glacial region. "This is a disaster. How such heavy machines reach our glaciers of Kashmir?" he wrote on X. The Environmental Policy Group (EPG) also expressed concern over reports of heavy machinery operating near Sheshnag Lake, describing the reported activity as a matter requiring immediate scrutiny by competent authorities. EPG convener Faiz Bakshi said Sheshnag was no ordinary water body but a glacial lake surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes, making it particularly vulnerable to human intervention. "Disturbing such terrain with heavy machinery is an invitation to disaster," he said. Referring to the visuals circulating on social media, Bakshi called for a public explanation regarding the nature of the work, the agencies involved, the environmental safeguards adopted and whether the activity had been assessed for its potential impact on the fragile landscape. He said any intervention in the vicinity of a glacial lake must be approached with extreme caution, given the vulnerability of such terrain to slope instability, erosion and other environmental risks. Bakshi also linked the concerns surrounding Sheshnag to wider ecological pressures affecting Kashmir's wetlands, where reports of excavation and disturbance at Shallabugh have caused apprehension amid the arrival of migratory birds. Jammu and Kashmir Students Association national convenor Nasir Khuehami also condemned the reported activity, warning that indiscriminate construction in fragile alpine areas could have serious ecological consequences. He sought details of the permissions and environmental clearances obtained for the work and called for accountability for any damage caused. Religious leader Muhammad Sameer Shafi Siddiqui also questioned the use of heavy machinery near the lake, citing the diminishing glacial cover in the Kolahoi region and elsewhere in Kashmir. "Given the already diminishing glacial cover at Kolahoi and other places, one fails to understand how such heavy machines are cutting into our already fragile ecosystem, and this time near such a pristine high-altitude glacial lake," Siddiqui wrote on X. He also highlighted the lake's importance for downstream water supplies, saying a large population depended on the Lidder River for drinking water and irrigation. Located at around 11,800 feet above sea level, Sheshnag is a glacier-fed lake measuring about 1.1 km in length and 0.7 km in width. It is a major stopover for pilgrims travelling from Chandanwari towards the Amarnath Cave, around 18-20 km away. The macadamised road ends at Chandanwari, beyond which pilgrims have traditionally travelled on foot, ponies or palanquins. The lake feeds the Eastern Lidder, one of the two main tributaries of the Lidder River. The other, the Western Lidder, originates from Kolahoi Glacier and flows through Lidderwat in the Aru region. The two streams meet at Pahalgam to form the main Lidder River. The river flows through Anantnag district before joining the Jhelum near Mirgund-Khanabal. Its waters sustain downstream communities and support drinking water supplies and irrigation across the Lidder basin. Sheshnag is among 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir. Authorities have conducted expeditions to vulnerable lakes, including Sheshnag, to assess potential risks and strengthen preparedness. The controversy has brought renewed attention to the environmental implications of infrastructure development in the fragile Himalayan region, with political parties, environmental groups, civil society representatives and religious leaders seeking clarity on the work and demanding an independent assessment of its potential impact on Sheshnag Lake and the Lidder basin.

"We've seen enough disasters over the years to understand how fragile mountain terrain is.
At some point, we really need to question whether such constructions are even worth it," he said.
Climate activist and RTI campaigner Raja Muzaffar Bhat questioned how heavy machinery had reached the glacial region.
"This is a disaster.

How such heavy machines reach our glaciers of Kashmir?" he wrote on X. The Environmental Policy Group (EPG) also expressed concern over reports of heavy machinery operating near Sheshnag Lake, describing the reported activity as a matter requiring immediate scrutiny by competent authorities.
EPG convener Faiz Bakshi said Sheshnag was no ordinary water body but a glacial lake surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes, making it particularly vulnerable to human intervention.
"Disturbing such terrain with heavy machinery is an invitation to disaster," he said.

Referring to the visuals circulating on social media, Bakshi called for a public explanation regarding the nature of the work, the agencies involved, the environmental safeguards adopted and whether the activity had been assessed for its potential impact on the fragile landscape.

He said any intervention in the vicinity of a glacial lake must be approached with extreme caution, given the vulnerability of such terrain to slope instability, erosion and other environmental risks.

Bakshi also linked the concerns surrounding Sheshnag to wider ecological pressures affecting Kashmir's wetlands, where reports of excavation and disturbance at Shallabugh have caused apprehension amid the arrival of migratory birds.

Jammu and Kashmir Students Association national convenor Nasir Khuehami also condemned the reported activity, warning that indiscriminate construction in fragile alpine areas could have serious ecological consequences.
He sought details of the permissions and environmental clearances obtained for the work and called for accountability for any damage caused.
Religious leader Muhammad Sameer Shafi Siddiqui also questioned the use of heavy machinery near the lake, citing the diminishing glacial cover in the Kolahoi region and elsewhere in Kashmir.

"Given the already diminishing glacial cover at Kolahoi and other places, one fails to understand how such heavy machines are cutting into our already fragile ecosystem, and this time near such a pristine high-altitude glacial lake," Siddiqui wrote on X. He also highlighted the lake's importance for downstream water supplies, saying a large population depended on the Lidder River for drinking water and irrigation.
Located at around 11,800 feet above sea level, Sheshnag is a glacier-fed lake measuring about 1.1 km in length and 0.7 km in width.
It is a major stopover for pilgrims travelling from Chandanwari towards the Amarnath Cave, around 18-20 km away.
The macadamised road ends at Chandanwari, beyond which pilgrims have traditionally travelled on foot, ponies or palanquins.
The lake feeds the Eastern Lidder, one of the two main tributaries of the Lidder River.
The other, the Western Lidder, originates from Kolahoi Glacier and flows through Lidderwat in the Aru region.
The two streams meet at Pahalgam to form the main Lidder River.
The river flows through Anantnag district before joining the Jhelum near Mirgund-Khanabal.
Its waters sustain downstream communities and support drinking water supplies and irrigation across the Lidder basin.
Sheshnag is among 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir.
Authorities have conducted expeditions to vulnerable lakes, including Sheshnag, to assess potential risks and strengthen preparedness.

The controversy has brought renewed attention to the environmental implications of infrastructure development in the fragile Himalayan region, with political parties, environmental groups, civil society representatives and religious leaders seeking clarity on the work and demanding an independent assessment of its potential impact on Sheshnag Lake and the Lidder basin.
